title: Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time

problem.claim: Video recommendation relies on logged watch time, but watch-time prediction is distorted by duration bias and may not accurately reflect user interests.

gap.claim: Existing label-correction methods treat completely played videos as equally high interest, despite variation in users' explicit feedback proportions for such videos.

contributions.claim: The paper introduces counterfactual watch time, defined as the potential time a user would spend watching a video if its duration were sufficiently long.
It proposes a Counterfactual Watch Model that relates counterfactual watch time to the time users obtain maximum benefit from video recommender systems.
It defines a cost-based transformation from counterfactual watch time to estimated user interest and trains the model with a counterfactual likelihood over observed watch times.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that analysis attributes duration bias to truncation of counterfactual watch time by video-duration limits, usually for completely played records.

The authors report that experiments on three real video recommendation datasets and online A/B testing showed improved recommendation accuracy and reduced duration bias with the Counterfactual Watch Model.

narrative_sequence.summary: Video recommendation uses logged watch time to address personalized information needs.
Watch-time prediction is affected by duration bias, and existing correction methods mishandle completely played records.
The authors attribute the bias to truncation of counterfactual watch time by video duration.
The paper introduces counterfactual watch time, proposes a model for it, and transforms it into user-interest estimates through counterfactual likelihood optimization.
The authors report gains in recommendation accuracy and reduced duration bias in dataset experiments and online A/B testing.

source_observation.claim: Observed watch time can be truncated by the video's duration, especially when users watch the entire video.

interpretation.claim: Behavioral measurements may confound user preference with exposure or measurement limits.

application.claim: For bounded engagement signals, model the latent counterfactual behavior that would occur without the limiting condition before estimating user interest.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach generalizes beyond video watch time or duration-limited engagement signals.

unknowns: The abstract does not name the three datasets.
The abstract provides no quantitative accuracy gains, bias reductions, or A/B-test details.
The abstract does not specify the counterfactual likelihood formulation or model architecture.
